questions.q: Why does this lesson argue a design review is necessary even when a design compiles and passes a quick test?
options: Because asynchronous bugs often only show up under real production volume, months after a quick sandbox test with a handful of records passed
Because Apex code never actually compiles correctly the first time
Because Salesforce requires a formal design review before any code can be deployed
Because quick tests are technically forbidden for asynchronous Apex
questions.explain: A design that works fine against a small test dataset can still fail at real production volume — asynchronous Apex's failure modes (limits, chaining, error handling) tend to surface under load, not in a quick functional test.

questions.q: A proposed design calls a future method, passing the full Contact sObject as a parameter. What does running this through the design-review checklist immediately reveal?
options: The design is fine as described and needs no changes
Future methods cannot accept an sObject parameter at all — this design won't compile, and should either pass the Id and re-query, or switch to Queueable Apex
The design only fails if the org has more than 100 Contacts
sObjects are allowed in future methods only if annotated with @future(sobject=true)
questions.explain: Future methods only accept primitive types, arrays of primitives, or collections of primitives (Lesson 3) — passing a Contact sObject directly won't compile. The fix is passing the Id and re-querying inside the method, or switching to Queueable Apex, which can accept the sObject directly.

questions.q: Per the checklist's 'Limits budget' item, what should a reviewer check for a recurring job or a chain?
options: Whether anyone has calculated the design's share of the shared daily asynchronous execution limit, especially at full production volume
Whether the Apex class name follows a specific naming convention
Whether the job uses exactly 200 as its batch chunk size
Whether the job was written using camelCase or snake_case variable names
questions.explain: The limits-budget checklist item asks whether the design's consumption of the shared daily asynchronous execution limit (Lesson 11) has actually been calculated — a design that looks fine in a sandbox can become an outage risk at full production scale.

questions.q: According to the checklist's 'Chaining safety' item, what should a reviewer confirm about any chained Queueable design?
options: That there's an explicit stopping condition checked before each chain call, and that Test.isRunningTest() guards the chain call
That the chain never goes deeper than exactly one link
That the chain only runs between midnight and 6 AM
That every chained job implements Database.Stateful
questions.explain: Chaining safety (Lesson 7) requires an explicit stopping condition checked before each System.enqueueJob call to prevent runaway chains, and a Test.isRunningTest() guard so the chaining code can actually be tested.

questions.q: A reviewed design has a Scheduled Apex job whose execute method loops directly over 3 million Account records with no Batch Apex involved. Which checklist item does this most clearly fail?
options: Tool choice — Scheduled Apex's execute method runs under synchronous-style limits and isn't built to process millions of records directly; this volume calls for Batch Apex
This design passes every checklist item as described
Only the chaining-safety item is relevant here, since no chaining is involved
Only the test-coverage item applies, since the other six items don't apply to Scheduled Apex
questions.explain: Scheduled Apex's execute method runs under governor limits comparable to a synchronous transaction, so looping directly over millions of records there fails the tool-choice checklist item — this volume needs Batch Apex, which the scheduled job should instead kick off.
